prompt: Put the five steps of vulnerability management in order, starting from the one everything depends on.
Why do organisations that scan every week still carry findings that are years old?

choices.text: Because scanners miss most flaws on their first run
choices.why: Finding them is not the problem here; acting on them is.

choices.text: The steps after the report get skipped
choices.why: Right: prioritising, fixing and verifying, with owners and dates.

choices.text: Because old flaws cannot be fixed once a newer version exists
choices.why: Old flaws are fixed by updates all the time.

choices.text: Because every report lists the same findings twice
choices.why: Duplication is a nuisance, not the cause.

prompt: Ubuntu ships a security fix for OpenSSH 9.6p1. Which part of the package version changes?

choices.text: The upstream part, which becomes 9.7
choices.why: Ubuntu backports the fix into the version it shipped.

choices.text: The epoch, which goes from 1: to 2:
choices.why: The epoch changes only when version numbering itself is reset.

choices.text: The packaging revision, such as 3ubuntu13.20 becoming 3ubuntu13.21
choices.why: Right, which is why only the full version string can be compared.

choices.text: Nothing: the same version is rebuilt with the fix
choices.why: A changed package always gets a new version, or apt would not install it.

prompt: Why does vulncheck.py call dpkg --compare-versions instead of comparing the two strings in Python?

choices.text: Because Python cannot compare strings that contain colons
choices.why: It can; the result would just be wrong.

choices.text: Because dpkg is faster than Python
choices.why: It is slower, one process per comparison, and still the right choice.

choices.text: As text, 13.9 sorts after 13.20; dpkg knows Debian's rules
choices.why: Right, and it handles the epoch too.

choices.text: Because the feed stores versions as numbers, not text
choices.why: They are strings in the feed.

prompt: Two advisories show `fixed` for web. Why is it right that a report does not raise them?

choices.text: web already runs a version newer than the fix
choices.why: Right, and listing them anyway teaches people to skim.

choices.text: Because those packages are not installed on web
choices.why: That would say not installed; these are installed and newer.

choices.text: Because their scores are below 7
choices.why: sudo's flaw scores 7.8; the version decides, not the score.

choices.text: Because the feed marked them as invented
choices.why: The whole feed is invented for the lesson; that does not decide anything.

prompt: What makes vulncheck.py an authenticated check?

choices.text: It asks for a password before it runs
choices.why: It asks nobody; it logs in with a key.

choices.text: It verifies the signature of the advisory feed before using it
choices.why: It does not; a real tool should, and that is another matter.

choices.text: It runs as root on web
choices.why: It runs as ana on admin.

choices.text: It logs in to web and reads the package database
choices.why: Right, instead of guessing from what services say.

prompt: An unauthenticated scan reads `nginx 1.24.0 (Ubuntu)` on web. Why can it not say whether a given nginx flaw is fixed?

choices.text: Because nginx encrypts its banner
choices.why: The banner is plain text in the response.

choices.text: Ubuntu fixes it in the packaging revision, which the banner does not show
choices.why: Right. A patched and an unpatched nginx say the same thing.

choices.text: Because nmap only reads the first port of each machine
choices.why: It read both ports asked for.

choices.text: Because port 80 is closed to admin
choices.why: It answered with a version.

prompt: If authenticated checks know more, what is an outside scan still good for, according to the lesson?

choices.text: Measuring the CVSS score of each service
choices.why: A score belongs to a flaw, not to a service it can see.

choices.text: Installing patches on machines with no agent
choices.why: Scanners report; they do not patch.

choices.text: Finding listeners nobody knew about
choices.why: Right, lesson 1's use of it.

choices.text: Proving that a hidden banner keeps the machine safe
choices.why: Hiding the banner blinds the defender's scan too.

prompt: What is OVAL, as the lesson describes it?

choices.text: Machine-readable advisories that distributions publish
choices.why: Right: the real form of this lesson's feed.

choices.text: A commercial scanner sold by Tenable
choices.why: That is Nessus.

choices.text: The probability that a flaw will be exploited in 30 days
choices.why: That is EPSS.

choices.text: A list of flaws known to be exploited in real attacks
choices.why: That is KEV.

prompt: Using cvss.py's formula, what base score does AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N get? (The transcript shows it.)
The sudo flaw has High impact on all three and scores 7.8, below the 9.8 of the full-control example. Which metric holds it down?

choices.text: S:U, because an unchanged scope always halves the score
choices.why: The full-control example is S:U too.

choices.text: AV:L, with PR:L: somebody must already be logged in
choices.why: Right. Exploitability falls; impact stays the same.

choices.text: UI:N, because no user interaction lowers the score
choices.why: UI:N raises exploitability; UI:R lowers it.

choices.text: A:H, because availability counts less than confidentiality
choices.why: The three impacts have the same weights.

prompt: Which of these does a CVSS base score know about?

choices.text: Whether the flaw is being exploited this week
choices.why: That is KEV and EPSS, outside the base score.

choices.text: Whether the package listens on your network
choices.why: That is exposure, which only you know.

choices.text: Whether an attacker needs an account
choices.why: Right: PR, privileges required, is one of the eight.

choices.text: How important the machine is to the firm
choices.why: Asset criticality is the firm's, not the flaw's.

prompt: Match each part of a CVSS vector with its question.

pairs.right: from where can it be reached?
must the attacker already have an account?
does it reach beyond the vulnerable component?

prompt: Why does prioritise.py put nginx (7.5) ahead of OpenSSH (8.1)?

choices.text: Because nginx listens on port 80, which is more exposed than 22
choices.why: Both are in EXPOSED; the policy does not rank ports.

choices.text: Its flaw is on the known-exploited list
choices.why: Right: KEV beats every score.

choices.text: Because the portal stops without nginx, and SSH is optional
choices.why: The policy does not weigh that; the kev field decides.

choices.text: Because its EPSS rounds up to 0.5
choices.why: 0.41 is not rounded, and kev is checked before EPSS.

prompt: Why does the small size of the KEV list, against all published CVEs, argue for using it?

choices.text: Because a short list is cheaper to download
choices.why: Size of the download is not the argument.

choices.text: Because CVEs not on the list cannot be exploited
choices.why: They can; there is just no evidence yet that they are.

choices.text: Most flaws are never used, so known use is a strong signal
choices.why: Right. Treating every 7.5 as urgent spends weeks on the wrong ones.

choices.text: Because every entry on it scores 9 or more
choices.why: KEV is about use, not score; nginx's entry here is 7.5.

prompt: How does the lesson remediate the vsftpd finding, and how does it prove it?

choices.text: It upgrades vsftpd and runs nmap again
choices.why: The lab has no newer vsftpd to install, and the portal does not need FTP.

choices.text: It purges the package and reruns vulncheck.py
choices.why: Right: not installed, the strongest answer.

choices.text: It adds an exception with an expiry date
choices.why: An exception is for what cannot be fixed yet; this could be removed.

choices.text: It blocks port 21 at the switch
choices.why: That would be a compensating control, not removal.

prompt: Under the lesson's policy, how many days does a P2 finding have?
Why are due dates counted from the day of the finding rather than the day of the report?

choices.text: So a reprinted report still shows what is late
choices.why: Right: otherwise the date moves every time.

choices.text: Because reports are always printed on the same day as the scan
choices.why: They are not, which is the whole problem.

choices.text: Because a later date would give the team more time
choices.why: That is the failure, not the reason.

choices.text: Because CVSS requires it
choices.why: CVSS says nothing about deadlines.

prompt: Which fields must an exception record carry, according to the lesson? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: an expiry date
choices.why: Without one, the finding becomes permanent.

choices.text: a compensating control
choices.why: What is done instead of the fix.

choices.text: who approved it, by name
choices.why: A decision somebody owns.

choices.text: the CVSS score raised by one point
choices.why: Nobody changes the score of a flaw.

prompt: A manager wants one number to judge the team each month. Which does the lesson recommend?

choices.text: The total number of open findings
choices.why: It rises with every new advisory, which the team does not control.

choices.text: The highest CVSS score still open
choices.why: One finding says little about the programme.

choices.text: The number of scans run in the month
choices.why: Scanning is one step of five.

choices.text: The count of findings past their due date
choices.why: Right: the one the team controls.

prompt: python3.12's advisory scores 9.8 with EPSS 0.11 but was `fixed` on web. If web had an older python3.12, which level would prioritise.py give it?

choices.text: P1, because 9.8 is the highest score in the feed
choices.why: P1 is for kev only.

choices.text: P2, because its EPSS is at least 0.10
choices.why: Right: the EPSS rule comes before the score rules.

choices.text: P3, because python3.12 is not in EXPOSED
choices.why: It would reach the EPSS rule first.

choices.text: None: a fixed package is never prioritised
choices.why: The question says the version is older, so it would be vulnerable.

prompt: The catalogue of flaws with evidence of exploitation in real attacks, kept by CISA, is called ___.
Match each signal with what it measures.

pairs.right: how bad the flaw would be
how likely exploitation is in 30 days
whether it can be reached here

right_distractors: how long the patch takes to install

prompt: After a patch is installed, what counts as verification in this lesson?

choices.text: The administrator's note that the patch was applied
choices.why: A note is a claim; the check is the evidence.

choices.text: A new nmap scan showing the same banner
choices.why: The banner does not change when Ubuntu patches nginx.

choices.text: The same check that found it now saying fixed
choices.why: Right: measured the way it was found.

choices.text: A lower CVSS score in the feed
choices.why: Scores describe the flaw and do not move when you patch.
